quests.instruction: Identify the emphasis. Your teacher says: "Water boils at ninety degrees." You politely correct her:
quests.word: Water boils at a hundred degrees.
quests.textToSpeak: Water boils at a hundred degrees.
quests.hint: The unit is already in the teacher's sentence. Which word is the one she got wrong?
quests.explanation: DEGREES was already in her statement, so it is shared ground. HUNDRED replaces her number and takes the peak, even though the sentence keeps going.
quests.emphasisRule: In a correction, the replaced word takes the peak and the repeated unit falls.

quests.instruction: Identify the emphasis. A friend says: "Isn't Sydney the capital of Australia?" You answer:
quests.word: Canberra's the capital.
quests.textToSpeak: Canberra's the capital.
quests.hint: Your friend has the idea right but the city wrong. Where does your voice go?
quests.explanation: The topic, 'capital', came from your friend, so it is old. CANBERRA'S supplies the fix and takes the peak at the very start.
quests.emphasisRule: When you correct a name, the new name carries the peak even if it opens the sentence.

quests.instruction: Identify the pitch pattern. A says: "Rohan wrote the quarterly report." B replies. What is B correcting?
quests.word: Rohan reviewed the quarterly report.
quests.textToSpeak: Rohan reviewed the quarterly report.
options: What Rohan did with the report
quests.correctAnswer: What Rohan did with the report
quests.hint: Compare B's sentence with A's. Only one word has changed. Which?
quests.explanation: Between the two sentences only the verb differs, and B's peak lands on REVIEWED. So the correction is about Rohan's role, not about the report or its name.
quests.emphasisRule: The peak falls on whichever word differs from the sentence being corrected.

quests.instruction: Identify the emphasis. A post office clerk asks: "Is the parcel for Mr. Dube?" You answer:
quests.word: It's for Mr. Dube's wife.
quests.textToSpeak: It's for Mr. Dube's wife.
quests.hint: The clerk had the family name right. What did he get wrong?
quests.explanation: The family name is shared, so DUBE'S is only a pointer. WIFE is the new information, and it takes the peak at the end of the possessive phrase.
quests.emphasisRule: Within a repeated name phrase, only the changed part takes the peak.

quests.instruction: Identify the emphasis. A parent says: "Ms. Iyer teaches the eighth grade, right?" The receptionist answers:
quests.word: Mr. Khan teaches the eighth grade.
quests.textToSpeak: Mr. Khan teaches the eighth grade.
quests.hint: The parent has the class right but the person wrong. Which word replaces the person?
quests.explanation: Everything after the name matches the parent's own words, so it all drops. KHAN is the only new piece and gets the peak early.
quests.emphasisRule: When the rest of a sentence is accepted, the corrected person takes the peak and the remainder stays low.

quests.instruction: Identify the pitch pattern. What did the first speaker most likely say?
quests.word: Neha wrote the speech.
quests.textToSpeak: Neha wrote the speech.
options: I think Joel wrote the speech.
I think Neha read the speech.
quests.correctAnswer: I think Joel wrote the speech.
quests.hint: Work backwards from the peak. Which idea would NEHA be replacing?
quests.explanation: The early peak on NEHA says the person was the problem, so the first speaker must have named someone else. If the verb had been wrong, WROTE would carry the peak.
quests.emphasisRule: An early peak on a name suggests the earlier statement named someone different.

quests.instruction: Identify the emphasis. The pharmacist hands you cough syrup, but you wanted something else.
quests.word: I asked for the cough tablets.
quests.textToSpeak: I asked for the cough tablets.
quests.hint: 'Cough' is not what the pharmacist mixed up. Which word is?
quests.explanation: COUGH is the shared condition, so it stays low. TABLETS contrasts with syrup and takes the peak.
quests.emphasisRule: In a modified noun, the part that distinguishes it from the other option takes the peak.

quests.instruction: Identify the emphasis. A neighbour says: "I heard the delivery brought your groceries." You answer:
quests.word: The delivery brought a sofa this morning.
quests.textToSpeak: The delivery brought a sofa this morning.
quests.hint: The neighbour is wrong about what arrived. Where does your voice go for the right item?
quests.explanation: The time phrase adds colour but doesn't answer the neighbour's guess. SOFA replaces 'groceries' and carries the peak.
quests.emphasisRule: A time phrase after the object stays low when the object is the correction.

quests.instruction: Identify the pitch pattern. What did the first speaker most likely say?
quests.word: She plays the violin.
quests.textToSpeak: She plays the violin.
options: Does she play the piano these days?
quests.correctAnswer: Does she play the piano these days?
quests.hint: The peak sits on the last word. What kind of detail would the earlier question have asked about?
quests.explanation: VIOLIN is the key piece of new information, which suggests the question was about which instrument. A question about frequency would have produced a peak on a time word.
quests.emphasisRule: A peak on a noun answers a question that guessed a different noun.

quests.instruction: Identify the emphasis. The receptionist says: "Your vaccination is due next week." You answer:
quests.word: It was due last week.
quests.textToSpeak: It was due last week.
quests.hint: The receptionist and you agree on the unit of time. What is different?
quests.explanation: WEEK is the shared unit, so it is old. LAST changes the direction of time, so the peak lands on it.
quests.emphasisRule: A time word that flips earlier and later takes the peak when the unit is shared.

quests.instruction: Identify the emphasis. A friend says: "The show starts at six, doesn't it?" You answer:
quests.word: It starts at six thirty.
quests.textToSpeak: It starts at six thirty.
quests.hint: Part of your friend's time was right. Which part isn't?
quests.explanation: SIX matches your friend's version, so it stays down. THIRTY is the added piece that corrects it and takes the peak.
quests.emphasisRule: When a time is partly right, the new part takes the peak.

quests.instruction: Identify the pitch pattern. A says: "The exam is on Tuesday." B replies. What is B pointing out?
quests.word: The exam was on Monday.
quests.textToSpeak: The exam was on Monday.
options: The exam is on a different day
The exam has already happened; it is over
quests.correctAnswer: The exam has already happened; it is over
quests.hint: B uses a different verb form from A. Which word carries the pitch?
quests.explanation: WAS takes the peak, so B is correcting the timing of the whole event: it's in the past. If the day alone were the problem, MONDAY would carry the peak.
quests.emphasisRule: A peak on a tense word corrects when something happens, not just which day.

quests.instruction: Identify the emphasis. A visitor says: "The pharmacy is next to the bank, right?" You answer:
quests.word: It's next to the post office.
quests.textToSpeak: It's next to the post office.
quests.hint: The visitor has the relationship right. Which part of the location is off?
quests.explanation: NEXT TO matches what the visitor said, so it stays low. POST OFFICE replaces 'bank', and in this compound the first word carries the peak.
quests.emphasisRule: In a replaced compound place name, the first element takes the peak.

quests.instruction: Identify the emphasis. A guest asks: "Is the wedding in the temple?" You answer:
quests.word: It's in the garden behind the temple.
quests.textToSpeak: It's in the garden behind the temple.
quests.hint: 'Temple' is already in the guest's question. What is new?
quests.explanation: TEMPLE is a landmark both people know, so it sits low. GARDEN is the actual venue and carries the peak.
quests.emphasisRule: A repeated landmark falls after the new place word.

quests.instruction: Identify the emphasis. A coworker asks: "Is the meeting upstairs?" You answer:
quests.word: It's downstairs now.
quests.textToSpeak: It's downstairs now.
quests.hint: The meeting has moved, but the coworker only needs one piece of information. Which one?
quests.explanation: NOW explains that it has moved, but the correction is the place. DOWNSTAIRS replaces 'upstairs' and takes the peak.
quests.emphasisRule: Location words that reverse each other (up/down, in/out) take the peak when corrected.

quests.instruction: Identify the emphasis. A friend says: "The ticket's five dollars, right?" You answer:
quests.word: It's ten dollars.
quests.textToSpeak: It's ten dollars.
quests.hint: Currency is not the problem. What is?
quests.explanation: DOLLARS is the shared unit. TEN replaces the wrong amount and carries the peak.
quests.emphasisRule: A corrected amount takes the peak; the unit that follows stays low.

quests.instruction: Identify the emphasis. A friend says: "Add a teaspoon of salt." You check the recipe and answer:
quests.word: The recipe says a tablespoon.
quests.textToSpeak: The recipe says a tablespoon.
quests.hint: You are not disputing the recipe; you are disputing the measurement. Which word is it?
quests.explanation: RECIPE is only your evidence. TABLESPOON replaces 'teaspoon' and holds the peak.
quests.emphasisRule: A unit of measure that corrects another unit takes the peak.

quests.instruction: Identify the emphasis. A manager says: "Everyone passed the safety test." One of the staff answers:
quests.word: Most of us passed.
quests.textToSpeak: Most of us passed.
quests.hint: The manager's claim used 'everyone'. What does the staff member change?
quests.explanation: PASSED is the repeated action, so it relaxes. MOST narrows 'everyone', so it carries the peak at the start of the sentence.
quests.emphasisRule: A quantifier that scales back a larger claim takes the peak.

quests.instruction: Identify the emphasis. A friend says: "So you drove to Chennai on Friday?" You answer:
quests.word: I drove to Madurai on Friday.
quests.textToSpeak: I drove to Madurai on Friday.
quests.hint: Most of your friend's sentence is right. Which single detail is wrong?
quests.explanation: Everything else in the sentence matches the friend's version, so DROVE and FRIDAY stay low. MADURAI is the lone correction and takes the peak.
quests.emphasisRule: In a partial correction, only the wrong detail takes the peak; every accepted word falls.

quests.instruction: Identify the emphasis. A manager says: "The marketing team presented the plan in April." A colleague answers:
quests.word: The sales team presented it in April.
quests.textToSpeak: The sales team presented it in April.
quests.hint: The month is mentioned twice. Is it in dispute?
quests.explanation: APRIL is accepted, so it carries no peak even though it ends the sentence. SALES replaces 'marketing' and takes the peak.
quests.emphasisRule: Accepted details at the end of a sentence stay low in a partial correction.

quests.instruction: Identify the pitch pattern. A says: "The workshop on Monday is cancelled." B replies. How much is B correcting?
quests.word: The workshop on Monday is postponed.
quests.textToSpeak: The workshop on Monday is postponed.
options: Only the status is being corrected, not the day
The day and the status both changed
quests.correctAnswer: Only the status is being corrected, not the day
quests.hint: Count how many words in B's sentence receive a peak.
quests.explanation: There is a single peak, on POSTPONED. MONDAY stays low, so the day is accepted. Two peaks, one on MONDAY and one on the status, would mean both were wrong.
quests.emphasisRule: One peak means one correction; accepted details stay low.

quests.instruction: Identify the emphasis. A says: "Thanks for coming on Tuesday." B politely corrects her:
quests.word: I think it was Wednesday, actually.
quests.textToSpeak: I think it was Wednesday, actually.
quests.hint: The speaker softens the correction at the end. What does the voice still highlight?
quests.explanation: THINK and ACTUALLY soften the correction, but they aren't the point. WEDNESDAY still takes the peak, and a slight rise afterward keeps the tone gentle.
quests.emphasisRule: A polite correction keeps the peak on the corrected word and softens the ending.

quests.instruction: Identify the emphasis. Someone says: "You're from Delhi, aren't you?" You answer:
quests.word: Actually, I'm from Jaipur.
quests.textToSpeak: Actually, I'm from Jaipur.
quests.hint: An opener can signal a correction without taking the peak. Where does the peak go?
quests.explanation: ACTUALLY warns the listener that a correction is coming but stays light. JAIPUR carries the information and the peak.
quests.emphasisRule: Openers like 'actually' mark a correction; the corrected word still holds the peak.

quests.instruction: Identify the pitch pattern. What does the speaker mean by this pitch? A colleague just gave the wrong meeting time.
quests.word: I thought it started at four?
quests.textToSpeak: I thought it started at four?
options: A gentle correction posed as a question
A firm statement of the right time
quests.correctAnswer: A gentle correction posed as a question
quests.hint: A fall would sound final. What does the speaker's rise do instead?
quests.explanation: The rise at the end turns the correction into something the colleague can agree with, rather than an announcement. It lets the listener save face.
quests.emphasisRule: A rising ending on a correction softens it and invites agreement.

quests.instruction: Identify the emphasis. Someone hurries through a scheduling message and catches her own slip.
quests.word: We meet on Tuesday, sorry, Thursday.
quests.textToSpeak: We meet on Tuesday, sorry, Thursday.
quests.hint: The speaker has said two days. Which one should the listener write down?
quests.explanation: TUESDAY was the slip, so it gets no strong peak. THURSDAY replaces it and takes the peak.
quests.emphasisRule: In a self-correction, the replacement word takes the peak and the abandoned word is passed over.

quests.instruction: Identify the emphasis. A speaker changes her mind mid-sentence.
quests.word: I'll email you, or rather, call you.
quests.textToSpeak: I'll email you, or rather, call you.
quests.hint: She is changing a plan. Which verb is the plan now?
quests.explanation: EMAIL is the abandoned option, so it stays light. 'Or rather' signals the switch, and CALL takes the peak.
quests.emphasisRule: After a phrase like 'or rather' or 'I mean', the new word takes the peak.

quests.instruction: Identify the pitch pattern. What does the pitch tell you about the names?
quests.word: Send it to Alex, sorry, Alia.
quests.textToSpeak: Send it to Alex, sorry, Alia.
options: The first name is stronger, so the second is an afterthought
The second name is stronger, so it replaces the first
quests.correctAnswer: The second name is stronger, so it replaces the first
quests.hint: Compare how strongly each name is spoken. Which name is the speaker committing to?
quests.explanation: ALIA is spoken more strongly than ALEX, so it is the one that counts. ALEX was a slip, and 'sorry' flags it.
quests.emphasisRule: In a self-correction, the repaired word is stronger than the slip.

quests.instruction: Identify the pitch pattern. A says: "The post office opens at nine." B replies. What kind of reply is this?
quests.word: The bank opens at nine.
quests.textToSpeak: The bank opens at nine.
options: A plain statement of the time
A correction of which place is meant
quests.correctAnswer: A correction of which place is meant
quests.hint: Compare B's sentence with A's. What was kept and what was changed?
quests.explanation: Only the place changed and the time was kept, so the peak sits on BANK. A plain statement would peak on NINE.
quests.emphasisRule: A peak early in a sentence that repeats the other speaker's details signals a correction.

quests.instruction: Identify the pitch pattern. What does the speaker mean by this pitch? A friend asks: "Where does your aunt live now?" You answer, and the pitch peaks on the last word.
quests.word: She lives in Mysore.
quests.textToSpeak: She lives in Mysore.
options: A correction of a city someone mentioned
A plain answer; nothing is being corrected
quests.correctAnswer: A plain answer; nothing is being corrected
quests.hint: Look at what the friend asked. Is there anything to correct?
quests.explanation: The friend asked for new information, so MYSORE is simply the answer and takes a normal peak. There is no earlier wrong claim being fixed.
quests.emphasisRule: A final peak in an answer to a wh-question is a plain answer, not a correction.

quests.instruction: Identify the emphasis. A receptionist says: "Your appointment is with Dr. Mehta, right?" You answer:
quests.word: I'm seeing Dr. Mehra, I think.
quests.textToSpeak: I'm seeing Dr. Mehra, I think.
quests.hint: The two names sound almost the same. Which one needs the clearest peak?
quests.explanation: The names are similar, so the listener needs the difference to be obvious. MEHRA takes the peak, and 'I think' is just a hedge afterwards.
quests.emphasisRule: When two similar names are being separated, the corrected one takes the peak and any hedge afterwards stays low.
